column3: Repeats the full warning-or-no-warning formula and identifies persistent disbelief as its outcome.
Its guided straight route does not clarify why warning fails to affect the addressed people.
Its comparison of unequal agents offers only a remote use of equality, not warning efficacy.
Closely restates the same structure: two different acts yield one result because refusal is settled.
The opening oath by the wise Quran grounds the message whose warning role leads into 36:10.
A shared word establishes common ground, but does not address an audience for whom warning is ineffective.
Shows denial generating accusations against the message, a concrete mode of the resistance in 36:10.
Identifies the addressee as a messenger, supplying the role from which the warning in 36:10 is issued.
A realized punishment scene validates prior warning generally, without explaining its failed reception.
Makes warning a direct messengerly command, supporting the act whose reception 36:10 qualifies.
Immediately defines the initially unwarned and heedless people to whom the mission is directed.
Places warning and reminder in the same revealed book while distinguishing their differing reception.
Its false alternatives about the messenger show rejection, but add little beyond that general pattern.
Records disbelievers' astonishment that a warner came from among them, explaining one resistant response.
Its equal notification supports the public character of warning, though not the no-effect result.
Its denial of equivalence between believer and defiant person supplies a broader outcome contrast.
Immediately states that warning reaches those who follow the reminder and fear the Merciful, sharpening 36:10's limit.
Its account of the soul's formation does not materially clarify warning or entrenched disbelief here.
The demand for a sign and response to revelation suggest resistance, but only indirectly.
The straight path immediately characterizes the message that is nevertheless refused in 36:10.
Contrasting responses to favor loosely parallels divided reception, without a specific warning connection.
Its judgment scene does not add a clear account of warning efficacy or disbelief.
Identifies the revelation's merciful and mighty source, supplying nearby context for the warning.
Equal public notice in treaty rupture is a distinct legal setting from the warning in 36:10.
Its rejoicing in divine favor has no clear bearing on the warning-or-no-warning result.
Its call to reflection on restoration only remotely relates to the presentation of a warning.
A temporary sign concerning speech does not clarify why listeners fail to believe.
Its description of believers' conduct offers little specific help with entrenched refusal.
The passage's commissioned-messengers scene begins the local example of how warning is resisted.
Its false equalization of other beings with the Lord is a possible cause of error, not the warning formula.
Its test of claimed equivalence concerns divine power rather than the reception of admonition.
Its revealed origin from the Merciful supports the authority of the message being rejected.
Its request for a straight way is guidance language without a direct link to failed warning.
Places warners among earlier peoples, broadening the recurrent historical setting of rejected warning.
The dispatch of multiple messengers directly supplies the local warning mission preceding 36:10.
The measured provision of sustenance does not materially illuminate warning or disbelief.
Defines the messenger's office as warning, directly supporting the action named in 36:10.
Its guidance onto a straight path has only a broad thematic relation to the warning mission.
Rejecting the message as poetry and reporting scant belief exemplify resistance to its authority.
Defines the messenger as only a clear warner, clarifying the bounded function in 36:10.
The local hearers deny the messengers and revelation, directly displaying the disbelief described in 36:10.
Deviation from the balanced path is only a distant account of error, not of warning's ineffectiveness.
Explicitly treats admonition and its absence as the same, closely paralleling 36:10's formula.
The oath by the glorious Quran establishes message authority but adds little after the nearer Quran context.
Its gentle familial guidance is a different reception scene and only broadly related.
Questions why people do not believe despite surrounding signs, supporting culpable nonresponse.
The messengers' reaffirmation of their commission directly continues the local resistance scene.
A retrospective warning-and-punishment refrain is general corroboration, not an explanation of the formula.
Its questions about reflecting on the Word and recognizing the messenger identify routes of refusal.
Guidance to a straight path is thematically related but does not clarify resistant hearers.
Its creation sequence does not add a clear connection to warning or belief.
Combines warning, heedlessness, and unbelief in a close parallel to the audience condition of 36:10.
The local messengers limit their responsibility to clear delivery, distinguishing delivery from acceptance.
Its security from fear has no positive connection to the warning's failed effect.
States that those upon whom the word has become due will not believe, closely explaining 36:10's closure.
A people reject proof and refuse belief in their messenger, an instance of resistant reception.
Its warning about exchanging faith for disbelief is a secondary route into the same outcome.
Its threat of divine seizure does not specifically address the reception of warning.
The hearers answer the messengers with threats, directly portraying hostility to reminder in the local scene.
Faith and righteous action identify an opposite response and its freedom from fear.
Limits effective hearing and guidance to those who believe in the signs, directly clarifying 36:10.
Pairs glad tidings and warning with turning away and not hearing, a close model of failed reception.
Its precise re-creation imagery does not materially illuminate warning efficacy.
Its denial that most hear or understand offers a close sensory picture of nonresponse.
The messengers reject the claim that their reminder is an omen, continuing the local refusal pattern.
Asks what discourse could produce belief after this one, strongly expressing exhausted receptivity.
Contrasts guidance for believers with deafness and blindness for nonbelievers, closely mapping differential reception.
The Quran's remembrance is relevant to message authority but adds little to the reception question.
Its creation and proportioning language does not clarify warning or unbelief.
States that the messenger can make hear only those who believe in the signs, directly paralleling the limit.
The local believer's call to worship presents the responsive alternative within the same episode.
Its agreed equal meeting-place is a separate use of equality, with no clear warning-efficacy contribution.
Failure to ponder the Word or recognize the messenger provides possible modes of rejection.
Pairs the messenger's clear warning with withheld timing knowledge, defining what warning does and does not provide.
Its account of the sky's formation adds no clear contribution to the focus ayah.
Reference to Moses' scrolls offers only a remote link to revealed communication.
The local believer rejects powerless intercessors, supplying a theological counter to the hearers' error.
Its creation account does not clarify why warning and non-warning yield the same result.
Questions disease, doubt, and fear in hearts, offering possible inner conditions behind refusal.
The disbelievers' surprise at a warner and accusations against him exemplify defensive rejection.
A completed punishment makes earlier warnings consequential, though it does not explain present ineffectiveness.
Links a revealed book, warning, and believing reception, forming a useful positive contrast.
The local believer identifies false worship as manifest error, clarifying the opposite of his responsive stance.
Its formation and human faculties do not directly explain why warning fails to move some hearers.
A recited book suffices as reminder for believers, contrasting receptive hearing with 36:10's closure.
Warns that ignored warning may be confirmed by a later event, a secondary consequence parallel.
Denies security from punishment, but has only an indirect relation to warning's reception.
Explicitly says signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe, directly corroborating 36:10.
The local believer publicly declares faith, presenting the response absent from the focus ayah.
Its creation and balancing sequence does not materially illuminate warning efficacy.
Describes believers increasing in faith when verses are recited, the positive reception contrast.
A sign for believers confirms that signs depend on a receptive audience, but only generally.
Its rhetorical challenge to disbelievers adds little beyond the already established rejection pattern.
The believers' final reward is an outcome contrast, not an explanation of present warning failure.
Its challenge to invented dietary prohibitions has no clear bearing on the focus ayah.
Links clear proofs, continued unbelief, and judgment in a historical instance of unresponsive recipients.
Its instruction on testimony and warning to the defiantly disobedient is a separate legal context.
Shows listeners who believe when the recitation reaches them, supplying a positive counterpart to 36:10.
Recounts messengers being denied or killed when their message opposed desire, a recurrent rejection pattern.
Immediately states that the word has become due over most of them and that they do not believe.
The immediately preceding image of bound chins and raised heads gives a concrete local picture of the closure behind 36:10.
The immediately preceding barriers and covering explain why the people cannot see despite the messenger's warning.
Defines the message as reminder and clear Quran, supplying the nearby content whose warning office is stated in 36:10.
Directly defines the Quran's purpose as warning the living, complementing 36:10's account of those who do not respond.
The sealing of hearts and hearing supplies a close explanatory image for warning that produces no belief.
Its deaf, dumb, and blind hearers cannot understand the call, closely portraying ineffective address.
Veils over hearts and deafness in ears directly explain why even signs fail to produce faith.
Restricts response to those who truly hear, closely matching 36:10's distinction between delivery and reception.
States that signs would not make them believe, a direct parallel to warning's failure to alter a settled response.
Describes hearts and sight being turned away after initial refusal, explaining the persistence of nonbelief.
Says former deniers would not believe in what they had previously denied, reinforcing entrenched refusal.
Describes hearts, eyes, and ears left unused for understanding, a broad account of unreceptive hearers.
Its whether-or-not formula produces the same result because forgiveness is withheld, a close structural counterpart to 36:10.
Questions whether the deaf can be made to hear when they do not reason, directly illuminating failed address.
Questions whether the blind can be guided when they do not see, a companion image of closed reception.
Says that every sign will not produce belief for these people until punishment arrives, extending 10:96's closure.
Attributes heedlessness to sealed hearts, hearing, and sight, a close account of why warning does not move them.
Describes a hidden barrier when the Quran is recited, directly relating recitation to obstructed reception.
Places coverings on hearts and deafness in ears so the Quran is not understood, closely explaining 36:10.
Combines being reminded of signs, turning away, veiled hearts, deaf ears, and never being guided.
States that the dead and deaf cannot be made to hear when they turn away, immediately preceding the candidate 27:81.
States that the dead and the turning deaf cannot be made to hear, directly complementing 30:53.
Distinguishes living from dead and makes hearing dependent on God's enabling, closely framing warning's limit.
Contrasts an opened breast with hardened hearts against remembrance, offering an inner-state account of resistance.
Reports covered hearts, deaf ears, and a barrier between messenger and hearers, a close rejection scene.
Describes desire followed by sealing of hearing and heart and a covering over sight, a strong closure parallel.
Its question about locks on hearts gives a compact image for the refusal to receive admonition.
The rusted-heart image offers a secondary account of accumulated resistance to message and warning.
